Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, won re-election to Alaska’s lone House seat Wednesday, surviving a Democratic wave that flipped both the Senate seat and the governor’s mansion.

Begich, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, defeated independent challenger Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman and retired teacher backed by the Alaska Democratic Party, following the state’s ranked-choice voting tabulation.

Begich’s victory, called at 9:27 p.m. ET on Wednesday – more than two weeks after Election Day – stood in sharp contrast to the rest of Alaska’s top-of-the-ticket results, where voters handed Democrats major breakthroughs despite Trump winning the state by 13% in 2024.

items.title: Ram through datacentres no one wants and hope the AI bubble never bursts: that’s the UK’s growth plan | George Monbiot
items.summary:
The government doesn’t know what they are going to be used for, but that’s beside the point. Their real purpose is to sustain the share price of big tech

It should have the status of an economic law: the sectors a government does most to promote in the name of growth are the sectors most likely to tank the economy. In the UK and the US, deregulation was meant to turn the financial sector into a never-ending growth machine. We have not yet fully recovered from the crash it helped cause in 2008. Fossil fuels are the most heavily subsidised sector on Earth. All that public money makes us highly vulnerable to oil price shocks, the whims of autocrats and societal collapse caused by climate breakdown. As for the great growth priority of our time – AI and datacentres – well, don’t take it from me. As Anthropic’s IPO prospectus warns, advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”.

One thing we learned from the US midterm elections is that the drive to build datacentres is less a function of real commercial demand than of the need to sustain the share price of the big tech companies. After citizens across the US voted for…

items.title: Andy Burnham is in danger of over-selling his big Brussels summit. What happens if he under-delivers? | Joël Reland
items.summary:
In laying a trap for himself, the PM could derail his longer-term ambition of revisiting Brexit

This week’s UK-EU summit may, one day, be seen as the start of the UK’s long march back towards the EU. Andy Burnham’s much-anticipated first meeting with EU chiefs in Brussels on Friday will be used to unveil a suite of detailed agreements to improve trade and economic cooperation, before the Prime Minister kickstarts his longer term “national conversation” about a much closer form of political and economic relationship with the EU. This, as Burnham signalled in a speech on Monday night, could well culminate in Labour’s next election manifesto abandoning the party’s famous red lines, and proposing an application for EU membership.

For pro-Europeans, this must read like a fever dream. Just four months ago, when Burnham took office, such a bold offer on Europe from the Labour party seemed implausible. But while Burnham has certainly reinvigorated the Brexit debate, he will have to move carefully to avoid storing up trouble for himself down the road. There is a risk that Burnham will come to be seen as someone who over-promises and under-delivers on Europe – and, in doing so, halts the growing momentum around revisiting the troublesome Brexit question.

Joël Reland is senior researcher at the…

items.title: Mullin defends TSA shoes-on policy after congressman calls classified briefing ‘very concerning’
items.summary:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended letting travelers keep their shoes on at airport checkpoints Wednesday after an Arizona congressman pressed him on why the TSA policy remains in place despite a classified watchdog review.

"We have never put anyone at risk at all," Mullin told Rep. Eli Crane, R-Ariz., at a House Homeland Security Committee hearing.

Mullin said the department evaluates screening technology daily and that he had personally met with DHS Inspector General Joseph Cuffari in a secure facility.

"In fact, we addressed three of the four concerns," Mullin said. He said the fourth, in his view, had nothing to do with security.

TLAIB MOVES TO BLOCK ICE AIRPORT ARRESTS, SAYS TSA HELPING TARGET IMMIGRANTS

Mullin gave no specifics about what DHS had done to address the three concerns or what the fourth involved.

Crane said he had received a classified briefing from the inspector general and called it "very concerning." He asked Mullin to discuss the matter privately.

items.title: Hundreds of subpoenas fly in DOJ’s ‘Decoy Dan’ probe as Democrat Peltola declared winner in Alaska
items.summary:
EXCLUSIVE: The Justice Department has issued more than 200 subpoenas in its criminal investigation into Dan J. Sullivan — "Decoy Dan" — who ran against Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, Fox News Digital has learned.

News of the scope of the sprawling criminal probe comes after Democrat Mary Peltola was officially declared the winner of the four-way general election on Tuesday night — two weeks after Election Day. She won 144,302 votes to the incumbent Sullivan's 131,844. A GOP candidate named Gerald Heikes won 6,105 votes, while so-called "Decoy Dan" won 4,760 votes as a non-party affiliated candidate.

A law enforcement source says the criminal case is continuing, and that Peltola being named the winner doesn't change anything from an investigative standpoint. The DOJ's investigation spans multiple states, and there are multiple criminal targets in the case, the source said.

A second source familiar with the investigation confirmed that more than 200 subpoenas have been issued.

Allegations have swirled that Democrats searched for a person with the name Dan Sullivan to run against the incumbent senator of the same name in order to confuse voters and potentially spoil the Republicans' chances of reelection.

Only 11 Democrats voted against Jeffries' nomination. Among those who opposed him — or intended to — were Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier, Adam Hamawy, Frederick D. Haynes III, Melat Kiros, Donavan McKinney, Chris Rabb and Claire Valdez.

In a joint statement, the group noted that discussions with Jeffries regarding their legislative priorities remain "ongoing."

"Whether on Medicare-for-all, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues," the incoming lawmakers said in their statement. "We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations."

items.title: Protesters heckle Trump's ex-Border Patrol chief offstage after Dem governor condemns College Republican event
items.summary:
Protesters heckled former Trump Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino off stage during a Monday night speech at Rutgers University, hours after New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill called the Rutgers College Republicans’ decision to host him "wrong" and urged the club to reconsider.

Bovino previously criticized Sherrill online, accusing her of prioritizing illegal immigrants over New Jersey residents. After returning to the stage, he called her "Sugar Pop Sherrill" and "Kim Jong Sherrill." Speaking to reporters afterward, he said she wanted to "trounce this freedom of speech," described the "Kim Jong Sherrill" label as "very fitting" and called the governor a "totalitarian." He also told Blaze News that Sherrill had timed her social media comments to "foment violence" against conservatives.

At Monday night’s Rutgers College Republicans event, protesters began shouting within minutes of Bovino taking the stage. Rutgers police escorted him offstage and ordered the hecklers to leave or face arrest, according to local reports. Bovino returned about ten minutes later to resume his remarks and answer questions. Hundreds of protesters also gathered outside.

items.title: 16 Ecuadorian fishermen sue US government, allege drone attack destroyed their boat near the Galápagos
items.summary:
More than a dozen Ecuadorian fishermen have sued the federal government, alleging they were wrongly targeted in a drone strike that destroyed their boat in the Pacific Ocean earlier this year as part of the Trump administration’s broader campaign against vessels suspected of drug trafficking.

The 16 fishermen aboard La Negra Francisca Duarte II say drones launched from a U.S. vessel struck their boat March 17, 2026, as they headed home from a two-week fishing trip near the Galápagos.

The strike set the boat ablaze, forcing the crew to jump overboard and escape in lifeboats, according to a lawsuit filed Monday in federal court in Pennsylvania. All 16 survived, but two suffered serious burns. One man’s leg was burned to the bone, the lawsuit says.

The fishermen’s lawyers say the crew had no ties to drug cartels or terrorist groups and posed no imminent threat when U.S. drones struck their vessel, which they say had been cleared by Ecuadorian authorities hours earlier.

The Tory leader is hardwired for conflict. It was futile for the PM to demand an end to her patronising tone

Well, that didn’t take long. When Andy Burnham first arrived in No 10, he said he was determined to do things differently. He wanted a new, consensual politics where he would work with other parties to put the country back together. Safe to say, that dream is already dead in the water. At least when it comes to his exchanges with Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions.

Andy might go through the motions of promising Ed Davey and various backbenchers a veneer of cross-party support that may or may not become reality – even Andy doesn’t have a clue which is which – but when it comes to Kemi, it’s now just a bloodless slanging match. Bloodless because there’s nothing really at stake. It’s all just a performance. Kemi has yet to land a blow on Burnham, so both leaders are merely playing to a gallery of their own backbenchers.

items.title: Recent service outages not state-sponsored attacks, DNI Jay Clayton testifies
items.summary:
Recent service outages across U.S. systems stem from routine technical and maintenance issues – not a coordinated foreign cyberattack, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton testified Wednesday, even as he warned lawmakers that "superintelligence" is rapidly escalating the speed and sophistication of future cyber threats.

"Based on what we know today, after a great deal of digital diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes, " Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee's "Worldwide Threats to the Homeland: 25 Years After 9/11" hearing. "They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack."

Clayton acknowledged public concern over the timing of the recent outages, telling the panel that the American people are right to ask questions, but intelligence reviews point away from foreign interference.

THE OUTAGES AMERICA HAS SUFFERED WEREN'T AN ATTACK, BUT THE NEXT FAILURE COULD BE

"We have no indication that these events are related," Clayton said in response to persistent questioning from Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y. "But let me answer something that the American people should know, which is the speed of compute and the level of capability of applications that use that compute is increasing substantially, which means legacy systems that were old six months ago or a year are a lot older."

The intelligence community remains…

items.title: Annoying Trump and dodging Flock: inside MapQuest’s contrarian comeback
items.summary:
After refusing to obey the president’s Lake Ontario order, MapQuest briefly rose to No 1 in navigation apps. It’s now a tool in the US anti-surveillance movement

I am among the legion of former PC desk occupants with warm memories of MapQuest, the Y2K-era travel website that kept millennial drivers on course with sheaves of printed-out directions – a quantum leap over the ungainly glovebox map. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech.

Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. Not only had it never signed off, MapQuest was reinventing itself as a plucky oppositional hero, the app most likely to uphold your geographical beliefs.

items.title: Milburn’s absurdly ambitious report offers blueprint for fixing everything and everyone
items.summary:
He lays out sweeping aims and finer details for how to fix the Neets crisis – and is obsessive about welfare

  • Neet ideas: what’s in Milburn’s report?

It is not clear if too many people were expecting Everything Everywhere All at Once, but that is what Alan Milburn has delivered. From a Welfare State to a Working State is almost absurdly ambitious. The terms of reference said something about the drivers of youth labour markets. We got a blueprint for how to fix everything and everyone.

What Keir Starmer, who commissioned it, had in mind, we’ll never know, but Milburn has taken up with gusto Andy Burnham’s general invocation to think boldly and rewire the state. Yes, it’s about training and jobs, but it’s also about pulling apart the NHS, giving schools and colleges an MOT, and once again, blowing up old-fashioned social security.
items.t: Milburn’s absurdly ambitious report offers blueprint for fixing everything and everyone

items.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
items.summary:
This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit.

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.

items.title: Hoping for Britain to rejoin the EU with Andy Burnham? You may be waiting a long time | Timothy Garton Ash
items.summary:
The PM’s first big speech on the UK and Europe was cautious and disappointing. Don’t expect any great leaps towards a new deal

Ever since Andy Burnham became the British prime minister this summer, people all over Europe have been asking me one question: “Will the UK rejoin the EU?” Sometimes they add: “And if so, when?” None of the intermediate options between the current hard Brexit and Brejoin are of any interest at all to most other Europeans.

Measured against these great expectations, Burnham’s first big speech on Britain and Europe, delivered on Monday evening amid all the pomp and circumstance the City of London could furnish, must be considered a disappointment. It was both a cautious and a curiously old-fashioned speech.

items.title: Should JD Vance run for president? I say go for it, habibi! | Arwa Mahdawi
items.summary:
Now the vice-president’s luck is turning, he seems reluctant to commit himself to the next presidential race – and I, for one, hate to see it

How do you think history will remember JD Vance? As the first vice-president to spark a vigorous debate about their eyeliner routine? As one of the last public figures to see Pope Francis alive? As the only politician in US history to have been the subject of a rumour about sexual relations with a couch (even though it was unfounded)?

I have no idea. But it seems increasingly unlikely he will be remembered as the 48th president of the US. After Maga’s midterm thrashing, Vance’s political future doesn’t look as bright as it used to. So much so that there has been a flurry of recent headlines debating whether or not Vance, once considered Donald Trump’s heir apparent, may slink away from a presidential run altogether.

The final week of Cop31 is in full swing, with just four days left to set a broad range of climate commitments into concrete action. I am on the ground at this year’s UN annual climate summit, where thousands of world leaders, businesses, nonprofits and scientists have converged in Antalya, Turkey, and there’s a lot left to do as the clock ticks down.

“Nearly 200 countries are working through 165 mandates,” executive secretary Simon Stiell told reporters at the midpoint on Saturday, pushing for a swift move to the hardest issues and championing compromise. “Each country has a view,” he said. “Every country has a voice.”
